title.full: Canada’s Energy Future 2026: Energy Supply and Demand Projections to 2050

description: Exploratory case with higher GDP growth, LNG exports, data-centre load and prices.
pathwayDescription:
The Higher scenario is one of two scenarios new in EF2026 that bracket Current Measures to explore economic and energy uncertainty. Keeping the same climate policies and technology costs, it assumes faster growth in four key drivers: real GDP (~2.0%/yr), LNG exports (three hypothetical projects, 8 Bcf/d by 2045), data-centre load (12 GW by 2050) and global oil and gas prices (Brent ~US$95/bbl). End-use demand is 12% above Current Measures in 2050, oil output peaks near 6.7 MMb/d, gas reaches 32 Bcf/d, electricity demand grows about 80%, and emissions end 9% above Current Measures (22% below 2005), gradually rising late in the period.

The CER is in charge of regulating construction and operation of energy assets and transport, export and trade of energy, exploration and siting activities. One of its responsibilities is to provide fact-based information on energy markets and supply as part of the Energy Information Program.

coreDrivers.policies: As in Current Measures, includes policies in place by Nov 2025. Carbon price covers industry and rises to $170/t by 2030, then flat. Clean Electricity Regulations push non-emitting generation above 96% by 2050 with clean Fuel, vehicle, efficiency, methane and HFC rules on top. Passenger ZEV represents 60% of sales by 2030, and 100% by 2035. Clean economy Investment Tax Credits lower CCUS, hydrogen and clean power costs.
coreDrivers.technologyCosts: Electricity capacity is chosen by a least-cost model, so unit capital costs steer the build. Baseline cost views from NREL ATB 2024, EIA and IEA decline from 2024 to 2050: onshore wind by 23%, solar by 38%, NG with CCUS by 24%, and SMR by 37%. Least-cost expansion under 80% higher electricity demand leans hardest on low-cost options: ~97 GW onshore wind added and 17.3 GW of SMRs by 2050, the largest SMR build of any scenario, plus 8.4 GW NG with CCUS.
coreDrivers.macroeconomicDrivers: Differentiating driver to Current Measures: stronger export demand is set to add ~0.4 pp/yr to real GDP growth versus Current Measures (2.0%/yr; population 0.9%/yr, reaching 52 M; CPI 2.3%). GDP is 11% above Current Measures in 2050, lifting end-use demand 12% and emissions 9%.
coreDrivers.otherDrivers: Higher market drivers: Brent ~US$95/bbl from 2030, Henry Hub to ~$6.75 by 2050. 3 LNG projects and 12GW of data center loads are needed by 2050.

dependencies.dependency_description: Identical policies (Clean Electricity Regulations, clean economy ITCs) must hold while generation grows ~80% and 12 GW of data-centre load is added; they still keep the grid over 96% non-emitting (power emissions −67% vs 2025). Policy strategy is shared only by the three current-policy scenarios: Current Measures, Higher and Lower but this pathways has more build out as it needs to meet higher demand. Hence, it relies more heavily on policy support.

The Clean Electricity Regulations’ compliance flexibility, including offsets, lets unabated gas run limited hours after 2050, but the largest gas fleet of any scenario (37.5 GW unabated in 2050) leans most on Clean Electricity Regulations compliance flexibility, so any MOU-driven change in Alberta would matter most here. Approval pace for ~200 GW of additions is not assessed.

Spending is the highest of the current-policy cases,  around $46 bn/year in avearge, peaking at $56 bn/year in 2041–45, about 75% above the 2006–2023 average. Prices still rise faster than inflation and financing that build at regulated rates is a major condition for the pathway.

The report does not model opposition. Indigenous engagement found communities favour renewables and some SMRs but want cultural sites preserved. The pathway experience more renewables construction but land is not a binding constraint neither.

As in Current Measures, behaviour is exogenous: the extra load comes from 12 GW of data centres and higher floorspace, not from consumer choice. Excluded demand-side management would matter more here given the highest variable-renewable share among current-policy cases.

The ~70% interprovincial transfer  expansion and 25.7 GW of batteries must handle 31% wind generation technology mix and 12 GW of data-centre load. The report states flexibility needs are ‘especially evident’ in the Higher scenario. US transfer capacity is fixed, distribution excluded.

The largest SMR fleet (17.3 GW, nearly three times more than in Current Measure scenario) plus 8.4 GW gas-CCUS, 6.5 GW hydrogen-fired and 25.7 GW of batteries (10% more than in Current Measure scenario). The firm-capacity build depends heavily on SMR cost reductions assumed equal to Current Measures.

Clean-power components depend on concentrated global supply chains (China provide more than 80% of solar modules, 70–80% of wind blades; graphite and lithium processing). The report doesn't provide any quantitative data for raw input needs for the Higher Scenario.

No hourly infrastructure is modelled for this variant, but with higher wind deployment, the system is obviously more dependent on wind availability, and gas would also fill demand during no-wind period. Hydro output would also vary with precipitation but the models do not otherwise include climate-change impacts.

Accelerating electricity installations could face skilled-labour shortages. Electricity Human Resources Canada projects 17,000–28,000 sector job openings in 2023–2028 against 110,600 jobs, and acute shortages could delay new generation and raise costs.

byMetric.scopeLimitations: Electricity economic-sector GHG, Mt CO2e, national only (no provincial split). Residual unabated gas runs under Clean Electricity Regulations compliance flexibility (p.51).

Installed capacity MW, Canada and provinces. Storage is battery only (‘Battery Storage’); pumped hydro is not separated and appears to sit within Hydro. No info on if captive or rooftop capacities are included in analysis. Includes wind dedicated to hydrogen production.

Derived: electricity-sector Mt CO2e (national inventory basis, direct, CO2e) ÷ total generation incl. distributed solar and wind dedicated to hydrogen; captive industrial generation not separately identified, so numerator and denominator may not align.
Generation GWh, Canada and provinces; includes distributed solar and wind dedicated to electrolysis. No info on if captive or rooftop capacities are included in analysis.
Capital and repair expenditure, C$2025, bulk power system only; excludes distribution and transmission other than generation connections and interties (p.88).
Overnight capital costs for onshore wind, utility solar, NG with CCUS and SMR; no storage, hydro or O&M costs disclosed; no cost file in the Open Government dataset.
Derived share of generation by technology (each technology ÷ ‘Total’); boundary as Generation.

Transfer capacity only stated in prose (~70% more interprovincial capacity by 2050 in all scenarios). Annual flows (not lines) are in electricity-interchange-2026.csv. Canada–US capacity fixed; distribution excluded.
